articles.summary: Thiago El Khory Rocha, de 28 anos, foi esfaqueado pelo suspeito de assediar a atendente do estabelecimento. Após o crime, o suspeito também foi agredido por moradores.
articles.body:
Thiago El Khory Rocha, 28 anos, foi morto a facadas após defender uma mulher de assédio em bar de Vila Velha, Espírito Santo — Foto: Reprodução/TV Gazeta

Um jovem de 28 anos foi assassinado na noite desta quarta-feira (21) dentro de um bar no bairro Santa Mônica, em Vila Velha , na Grande Vitória. Segundo testemunhas, Thiago El Khory Rocha foi esfaqueado após defender uma atendente do estabelecimento de um suposto assédio.

Gabriel Silva Paiva, de 38 anos, é apontado pela Polícia Militar como autor do crime. Após o assassinato, ele tentou fugir, mas foi agredido por moradores e ficou ferido. O homem foi socorrido pelo Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e levado para o Hospital São Lucas, em Vitória, onde ficou internado sob escolta policial.

Segundo moradores, Thiago e Gabriel passaram o dia bebendo no bar. Em determinado momento, Gabriel teria assediado a atendente, e Thiago decidiu defender a mulher.

As testemunhas contaram que os dois começaram a discutir e que Gabriel foi até casa, buscou uma faca e voltou ao estabelecimento, onde esfaqueou Thiago.

Após o crime, Gabriel tentou fugir pela Avenida Perimetral, no sentido do bairro Coqueiral de Itaparica, mas retornou e foi agredido pela população. De acordo com os relatos, ele foi espancado com cadeiras, mesas, pedras e pedaços de madeira.

Gabriel Silva Paiva, de 38 anos, é suspeito de matar a facadas o jovem Thiago El Khory Rocha, 28 anos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Gazeta

O estado de saúde do suspeito não foi informado.

A perícia da Polícia Científica esteve no bar para analisar a cena do crime. O corpo de Thiago foi encaminhado ao Instituto Médico Legal (IML), em Vitória.

A família da vítima esteve no local, mas, abalada, preferiu não gravar entrevista. Thiago deixou uma filha de seis anos.

Gabriel Silva Paiva foi autuado em flagrante por homicidío qualificado. Assim que sair do hospital, vai ser levado ao presídio. A arma do crime não foi encontrada pela polícia.

articles.summary: Acidente aconteceu no Córrego do Machado, em Palmas. O corpo da vítima foi levado para o Instituto Médico Legal (IML).
articles.body:
Raphael de Brito morreu após receber descarga elétrica ao mexer em fiação de casa — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

Um homem de 36 anos morreu após receber uma descarga elétrica na manhã desta quinta-feira (22), em Palmas . Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança Pública, a vítima estava manuseando fios de energia elétrica na própria casa quando levou o choque.

O caso foi registrado na zona rural da capital, próximo ao Córrego do Machado. O Instituto Médico Legal (IML) foi chamado e recolheu o corpo. A vítima foi identificada como Raphael de Brito.

articles.title: How a bullet’s twists and turns saved man shot during Tiger Shroff attack
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Umesh Chauhan (34), shot as a bystander during the attack on Tiger Shroff, survived thanks to the bullet’s unpredictable trajectory, said doctors.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Umesh Chauhan (34), shot as a bystander during the attack on Tiger Shroff, survived thanks to the bullet’s unpredictable trajectory, said doctors. Dr Harish Pathak, dean of KEM Hospital, where Chauhan was operated on, said the bullet’s extreme heat during firing would have sterilised it.Surgeons said it entered the lower left chest, below the heart, passed through the liver, grazed the lung and struck a right-side rib. The impact deflected it without fracturing the rib, slowing it before it lodged in the right posterolateral back muscle, near but not touching the spine.“He is a very lucky man. The bullet’s movement, how it turned, where it hit, all made a difference,” said Dr Uday Jadhav, head of cardiovascular & thoracic surgery (CVTS). “Its final position allowed extraction through just a 1.5-cm incision. A different trajectory could have required major surgery or struck the heart, proving fatal.”The operation involved teams from general surgery, CVTS, pulmonary medicine, hepatology, cardiology, radiology and anaesthesiology. Dr Pathak said a bullet’s diameter determines only the entry wound, not the full extent of damage. Chauhan’s liver has begun healing. articles.title: Marijuana use rises sharply among one group of Americans, new study finds
articles.summary: At least 5.9 million U.S. children lived with a parent who used marijuana on most days in 2024, a new study estimates, raising safety concerns.
articles.body: A growing number of American parents are using cannabis, prompting questions about potential child exposure and safety, according to a new study. Cannabis use increased substantially among parents between 2012 and 2024, with researchers estimating that at least 5.9 million U.S. children were living with a parent who used marijuana on most days in 2024. By 2024, 8% of parents used cannabis on most days, 5.2% used it daily and 6.7% met the criteria for cannabis use disorder (CUD). IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE Daily cannabis use among parents was about four times as common as daily alcohol use, the study found. While increases occurred across nearly all demographic groups, some of the largest were seen among younger and unmarried parents, those in lower-income households and those without a four-year college degree. Researchers from the University of California, San Diego, analyzed data from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH), involving nearly 482,000 U.S. individuals ages 12 and older. The findings were published in the journal Addictive Behaviors. MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS "Marijuana has become so socially acceptable that people are starting to overlook the risks," Dr. Jarid Pachter, who specializes in family medicine and addiction medicine at Stony Brook Medicine in New York, told Fox News Digital. "Just because it's legal doesn't mean it's harmless," added Pachter, who was not involved in the study. The physician also expressed concern about the example parents are setting for their children. "If marijuana use is a regular part of life at home, children may start to see it as something that's normal and relatively harmless," he said, pointing to studies that show children whose parents use marijuana are more likely to use it themselves as they get older. "Just because it's legal doesn't mean it's harmless." "That doesn't necessarily mean the parent's marijuana use is causing the child to use, but there's clearly an association." The doctor also cautioned that THC, the main psychoactive chemical in the marijuana plant, is known to affect attention, memory, coordination and reaction time. NIGHTLY GLASS OF WINE MAY NOT BE AS HARMLESS AS MANY PEOPLE THINK, STUDY SUGGESTS "When you have young children, you need to be alert and able to respond to their needs," he said. "I'm not suggesting that someone who uses marijuana can't be a good parent. My concern is about being impaired when you're responsible for a child's safety." "I also think we need to be careful about normalizing daily marijuana use," he went on. "We wouldn't automatically consider daily alcohol use harmless, and we shouldn't look at marijuana that way, either." Pachter emphasized that accidental ingestion is another concern, especially with edibles like marijuana gummies or chocolate, which can look like regular candy to a young child. "We've seen significant increases in emergency room visits involving children who accidentally consume marijuana," he told Fox News Digital. CANNABIS COMPOUNDS COULD REVERSE DISEASE AFFECTING ONE-THIRD OF ADULTS "Some develop severe sedation, confusion and difficulty walking. In more serious cases, children can have breathing problems and require hospitalization." The more frequently someone uses marijuana, the greater risk of developing cannabis use disorder, the doctor cautioned. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "We also know THC can affect memory, attention and coordination. Frequent use, particularly of high-potency products, is associated with an increased risk of certain psychiatric problems in susceptible individuals." Smoking marijuana around children can also pose a risk of secondhand exposure. "Marijuana smoke contains many of the same harmful chemicals found in tobacco smoke," the physician said. "We know children can be exposed to THC through secondhand smoke, although we're still learning about the long-term health effects." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER For those who use marijuana every day, Pachter suggests they ask themselves whether they can go without it, and whether it is affecting work, relationships or responsibilities. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "And if you're a parent, you need to consider whether your marijuana use is affecting your ability to care for your children." The study had some limitations. The researchers did not assess parenting quality or childrenâs health, and the findings do not establish that parental cannabis use causes adverse child outcomes. Additionally, the data relied on self-reported substance use, which could be subject to recall or reporting bias. The researchers called for further studies examining whether the frequency of parental cannabis use, cannabis use disorder, household exposure and storage practices are associated with childrenâs health or developmental outcomes. articles.title: Man drowns during Durga idol immersion in Maner
articles.summary: 25-year-old Shashi Kumar drowned during Durga idol immersion at Ramghat pond in Maner, Patna, after his foot got trapped; family alleges hospital negligence.
articles.body: Patna: A 25-year-old man drowned during the immersion of Goddess Durga’s idol at Ramghat artificial pond at Maner in Patna district late Wednesday night after his foot got trapped in the wooden structure beneath the idol, police said.The deceased, Shashi Kumar, son of Suresh Paswan, was a resident of Newati Mohalla. According to local residents, Shashi was participating in the immersion procession when he entered deep water along with the idol. His foot got stuck in the wooden structure, causing him to lose his balance and drown.Locals pulled him out of the water and rushed him to Maner Primary Health Centre (PHC), where doctors declared him dead. Hoping to save him, his family then took him to a private doctor before rushing him to ESIC Hospital in Bihta. However, doctors there also declared him dead.The family alleged that ESIC Hospital management did not provide an ambulance to transport the body, forcing them to return to Maner with it on a motorcycle.The family also accused doctors at the Maner PHC of negligence, claiming that Shashi was breathing when he was pulled out of the water but was declared dead without receiving proper treatment.Maner police station SHO Rajneesh Kumar said that, based on the report received from PHC doctors that Shashi died by drowning, police are conducting further legal proceedings in the case.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: Patna needs better healthcare access in underserved areas: CUSB study
articles.summary: CUSB study finds 4 in 10 Patna residents say hospitals are inadequate; GIS mapping identifies four priority zones for new public healthcare centres in underserved areas.
articles.body: Patna: Nearly four in every 10 Patna residents believe the city does not have enough hospitals, while even more are dissatisfied with the availability of hospital beds, according to a recent study conducted by the Central University of South Bihar (CUSB).The study, conducted jointly by CUSB geography department head Kiran Kumari and research scholar Akash Kumar, has identified four potential priority zones for setting up new public healthcare centres, with particular focus on underserved areas and the city’s expanding outskirts. The researchers said Patna needs more healthcare facilities to meet the needs of its growing population, especially in underserved areas.Published in the international journal Discover Public Health, the research, titled “Mapping spatial and socioeconomic disparities in public healthcare accessibility in Patna City,” is based on surveys of 384 respondents across six administrative areas. The journal is indexed in Scopus (Q4) and the Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI) of Web of Science. The study found that the presence of hospitals does not guarantee easy access to healthcare.The researchers found that people living far from hospitals were less likely to use public healthcare services, while better availability encouraged greater use. Income also influenced satisfaction with healthcare services.Using Geographic Information Systems (GIS), statistical analysis and socioeconomic surveys, the researchers mapped hospital locations against road networks, population density and land availability to identify areas where existing facilities may not adequately serve residents.Using GIS and statistical analysis, the researchers identified four potential priority zones around Ward Nos. 13–14, 20–23, 27 and 35–36. The analysis considered population density (29%), distance from healthcare centres (27%), underserved areas (22%), road connectivity (14%) and land availability (8%).The researchers suggested giving priority to areas on the city’s outskirts that lack adequate healthcare facilities. They also called for better transport and more awareness of govt health schemes. However, they said the proposed sites are only suggestions and need further assessment before new facilities are set up.Kumari said the study sought to understand the difficulties people face in accessing public healthcare and provide evidence-based inputs for policymakers. articles.title: Cardiologists Reveal the Healthiest Drinks for Your Heart and 2 to Avoid
articles.summary: The best drinks for heart health are water and other unsweetened beverages, American College of Cardiology guidelines note. Limit sugary drinks and alcohol.
articles.body: Be mindful about what you drink. It could affect your heart health and risk for cardiovascular disease. Sipping certain beverages adds sugar, chemicals and stimulants to the diet. The liquid calories provide less satiety than food, leading to overindulgence and weight gain. But fill your glass or cup with a healthy beverage and you can provide the body with the healthy hydration it craves. “If you’re well hydrated, your heart doesn’t have to work as hard,” the American Heart Association notes. Heart Health Tip of the Day: Prioritize These Beverages for Cardiovascular Wellness Water and other unsweetened beverages are the “preferred choice for long-term health,” the American College of Cardiology emphasized in its newest dietary guidelines, titled “Food and Health: Nutrition for Prevention and Management of Cardiovascular Disease.” Moderate amounts of coffee and tea, equivalent to two to five standard 8-ounce cups per day, appear to be safe for most people and are associated with a lower risk of cardiometabolic diseases, the authors add. The scientific statement urges people to limit or avoid two types of drinks: alcohol and sugar-sweetened beverages, which are “consistently” associated with a higher risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Dr. James Stone, a cardiologist at the South Heart Clinic in Harlingen, Texas, says he only drinks three liquids: water, black coffee and unsweetened tea. “Why? Because if we woke up 800 years ago, there’d be water. If we got tea leaves, we were lucky enough to have unsweet tea; and if we were lucky enough to find a coffee bean, it was black coffee,” Stone tells TODAY.com about his philosophy to stick to a diet that humans were engineered for over the course of centuries. Why It Matters Plain water tops the list of the healthiest drinks, says registered dietitian Natalie Rizzo, nutrition editor for TODAY. It has no calories and perfectly hydrates the body. Coffee and tea also make the list. Both contain caffeine plus polyphenols and other bioactive plant compounds since they come from plants. Drinking coffee and tea is associated with cardiovascular benefits, the American College of Cardiology notes. Just be aware that unfiltered coffee such as French press, boiled, Turkish and espresso raises LDL cholesterol, the type that clogs arteries, the guidelines caution. That’s because it contains cafestol — a cholesterol-raising compound found “abundantly” in coffee beans. A filter catches it, so a filtered brew is considered the healthiest coffee. If you’re a fan of diet drinks, the evidence on the long-term metabolic and cardiovascular effects of low-calorie sugar substitutes is “inconclusive,” the statement notes. Meanwhile, the relationship between alcohol consumption and cardiovascular health “remains controversial,” so alcohol should be limited or avoided, according to the guidelines. How to Get Started Reach for plain water — the perfect beverage for your body’s hydration needs. It can be flat, sparkling or served with a splash of 100% fruit juice added in for a little flavor. Coffee and tea in moderate amounts are also good options, just skip the cream and sugar. Avoid sugary beverages like soda. Higher intake is associated with heart disease risk regardless of physical activity levels and may raise the risk of dying from an obesity-related cancer. When it comes to alcohol, don’t start drinking it “for health reasons,” the guidelines advise; and if you choose to drink, do it in moderation — no more than one drink per day for women, two for men. Stone also advises patients to avoid energy drinks because they contain several stimulants — which can lead to potential heart rhythm issues — plus added sugar. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Family of toddler found alive in hospital morgue to file lawsuit: ‘I just want justice for my son’
articles.summary: Vincent Fiordilino was pronounced dead after he was found unresponsive in a swimming pool. A worker later observed him moving and breathing in a hospital morgue.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — An Arizona woman is sharing the story of how her toddler son was pronounced dead at the hospital early this year only to be found, hours later, stirring beneath a sheet in the morgue.

Eighteen-month-old Vincent Fiordilino was found unresponsive in a swimming pool on Feb. 8 and rushed to Dignity Health Mercy Gilbert Medical Center in Gilbert. After attempting to revive the child, medical staff made the formal call to pronounce him dead, even though some observers insisted they saw signs of life, the boy’s mother, Alexus Fiordilino said.

“A nurse or a doctor said that it was just agonal breathing, which, is like, I guess, a death gurgle,” she said during an interview on NewsNation’s “Jesse Weber Live” on Wednesday. “Through the grief of it all, I kind of just accepted that answer.”

John Brewer, the family’s attorney, said a transporter for the county medical examiner’s office later came to retrieve the boy’s body from the hospital morgue and encountered an alarming sight.

“Underneath the thick sheet, all four extremities — his arms, his legs — are moving,” Brewer said. “He turns to the security guard and says, ‘That kid’s alive,’ and (the guard) said, ‘No, doctor says that’s normal.’”

Child found ‘slightly moving and slightly breathing’

The driver examined the child, the attorney said, and insisted that security call for a nurse.

Fiordilino said she and her husband then received the startling news from a police detective that the boy was “slightly moving and slightly breathing” and was being transported to Phoenix Children’s Hospital.

Alexus Fiordilino said Vincent has a hypoxic brain injury that will require lifelong medical care.

Mother to file lawsuit: ‘It just destroyed our lives’

Brewer said a lawsuit would be filed against the hospital next week, but did not specify who else could be named as defendants.

“It just destroyed our lives, and we came to them for help,” Fiordilino said. “I just want justice for my son. I want my son to have the best life that he could.”

An attorney for the physician who Brewer says mistakenly pronounced the child dead released a statement saying the doctor’s thoughts are with the Fiordilinos. The legal representative declined to discuss the actions at the hospital, citing pending litigation.

Maricopa County prosecutors said over the summer they would not file charges against the parents.

“Gilbert Police submitted a recommendation of charges of Child Abuse for both parents. In this case, the family had multiple childproof locks and safety measures in place, and multiple adults were present in the home, all of whom believed someone was watching the child. Additionally, the investigation found no evidence that the parents exhibited any obvious signs of impairment,” officials said.

articles.title: Drug freebies benefit hospitals, traders, not patients: Chemists
articles.summary: Federation of Chemist and Druggists of Karnataka urges regulators to clarify “buy 1 get 1” drug freebie rules, alleging hospitals/traders benefit, not patients.
articles.body: Koppal: Pharmaceutical companies’ ‘buy 1 get 1 free’ offers are benefiting hospitals and large traders rather than patients, the Federation of Chemist and Druggists of Karnataka has alleged. It has sought clear rules to ensure that consumers receive the benefits of such schemes.In a representation to the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and other drug regulators, federation president Ashokswamy Heroor, in Gangavathi, sought clarification on how free medicines should be accounted for under the Drugs Prices Control Order (DPCO), 2013.The federation cited schemes such as Mankind’s Kit (one plus four free), Manforce (one plus seven strips free) and Prega News (one plus two free). It also cited Zydus’s Penegra (one plus one free), Abbott’s Fincef injections (10 plus 12 or 14 free) and Alkem’s Xone injections (10 plus 26 free).The key question, Heroor said, was whether the landing price should be calculated by averaging the cost of purchased and free medicines or whether the additional units should be supplied to patients free of charge. He alleged that hospitals and large traders retain the benefits of these offers, leaving patients without any relief.The federation also flagged medicines carrying steeply inflated maximum retail prices (MRPs) despite being supplied to retailers at low rates. It cited injections with a price to retailer (PTR) of Rs 30 but an MRP of Rs 312.4, and protein powders costing Rs 10-20 were allegedly marked at up to Rs 300.Such pricing allows chain stores to offer steep discounts, putting traditional medical stores at a disadvantage, the federation said. It sought an investigation into the practice and urged pharmaceutical manufacturers to lower MRPs and follow ethical business practices.The representation also alleged that pricing irregularities had increased since DPCO-2013 came into force. It urged drug control officers to examine Form-5 documents to verify compliance with the provisions governing maximum allowable post-manufacturing expenses (MAPE).The federation welcomed the Karnataka Food Safety and Drugs Administration Department’s Oct 1 circular directing hospitals, distributors, carrying and forwarding agents, stockists and traders to display landing/base prices and MRPs on bills. The directive is to be implemented from Nov 1, 2026.It sought strict enforcement of the circular, immediate revival of the dissolved DPCO Cell and restriction of the Licensing Authority’s powers to the Additional Drug Controller level. articles.title: ‘Longer we wait, worse it gets’: Struggle of Gaza’s breast cancer patients
articles.summary: Breast cancer patients in Gaza face delayed diagnoses, medicine shortages and limited access to scans and treatment.
articles.body:
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Hiba Musbah has already been through seven rounds of chemotherapy for the breast cancer that is plaguing her body. Next week will be the eighth.

But the 36-year-old mother of three, from eastern Deir el-Balah, says her condition has continued to deteriorate as she waits to travel outside Gaza for further treatment.

“I can no longer take care of my children as I used to. My son is the one who helps me,” she told Al Jazeera. Her husband Motaz, who has a heart condition, has had to take on more responsibility as her health has worsened, caring for their three children – Mohammed, 13, Jaber, 10, and Ahmad, eight.

Musbah first noticed lumps around her right breast in January 2024, a few months after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. At the time, she initially ignored them because she was displaced and the war was intensifying. Her mother eventually insisted that she seek medical attention.

Doctors confirmed it was cancer, but despite needing urgent surgery, it took two months for Musbah to be operated on, with the delay caused by Israeli military attacks around the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, where she was being treated.

“The situation was difficult, with the bombardment and the tanks,” she said. “I delayed the operation because of the war. The last time, I nearly died from tank fire, so I postponed the operation.”

Her chemotherapy was initially also delayed for seven months because medicines were unavailable at Nasser Hospital.

Musbah’s experience reflects the reality facing hundreds of women with breast cancer in Gaza, where Israel’s war and blockade have severely weakened the health system’s ability to diagnose and treat the disease.

Shortages of medicines and medical equipment, broken diagnostic machines, the absence of radiotherapy and difficulties leaving the Gaza Strip for specialised care have turned the fight against cancer into another struggle amid Gaza’s deepening health and humanitarian crisis.

Surgery, chemotherapy and the cost of waiting

The lack of access to diagnostic equipment is now another source of anxiety for Musbah. She explains that she needs a new computerised tomography (CT) scan to assess how her condition has progressed, but has been unable to obtain one because the equipment is unavailable at public hospitals.

A private hospital has a scanner, she said, but the examination costs about 150 shekels ($48), which she cannot afford. The waiting time for an appointment can also exceed three months.

“I am now suffering from pain in my back and leg, and I have not had a scan for three months because the equipment is unavailable,” she said. “My doctor told me he was concerned that the disease might have spread through my body, but I still do not know.”

Musbah now struggles to walk and move one of her arms, and experiences pain in her shoulder, legs and eyes, as well as damage to her hair and nails during treatment.

“If I had received treatment early, things would not have reached this point. My condition has become much more difficult because my treatment was delayed,” she said. “Cancer patients also need good food, fruit, meat, fresh produce, but we cannot afford everything we need.”

According to Musbah, she has been waiting for around two years to leave Gaza for treatment after receiving a medical referral. But Israel, which controls all entry and exit from Gaza , has yet to give her security approval to travel.

“I want to travel, receive treatment and get better,” Musbah said. “I want to regain my health and return to the way I was before.”

According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the Gaza Strip recorded about 360 new breast cancer cases annually before the war, compared with 250 in 2024 and around 260 in 2025.

The ministry has warned that these figures may not reflect the true number of cases because screening and early-diagnosis services have largely collapsed, potentially leaving hundreds of patients undiagnosed.

In a statement on October 1, the ministry said repeated breakdowns of mammography machines and shortages of laboratory supplies had severely restricted early detection in Gaza. Chemotherapy, hormonal and targeted therapies were also unavailable or critically scarce, while radiotherapy was completely unavailable.

The ministry said surgery for advanced tumours had also been halted because of a lack of specialised medical capabilities.

The shortage of diagnostic equipment adds another obstacle for women who suspect they may have cancer.

Dr Iman al-Haj Ahmad, an obstetrician and gynaecologist at Hikmat al-Jamei Health Centre in Deir el-Balah, understands these barriers both as a doctor helping women seek diagnosis and as a breast cancer patient herself, having been diagnosed in May 2025.

“I had to search until I found a place where I could get a mammogram,” al-Haj Ahmad said. “I kept thinking about ordinary women who don’t have the medical knowledge or connections that I have. If it was this difficult for me, how much harder must it be for them?”

Before the war, women could seek an initial examination at a primary healthcare centre and be referred to hospitals for mammography, ultrasound scans, and further tests.

Now, al-Haj Ahmad said, imaging services are limited, some cancer specialists have left Gaza, and tests needed to confirm a diagnosis are not always available through public health services. Some patients have to pay privately.

Al-Haj Ahmad waited about a month for surgery, eventually undergoing the operation at Nasser Hospital with a visiting Jordanian medical team while the hospital was operating under dangerous conditions.

Chemotherapy and severe food shortages later took a heavy toll on al-Haj Ahmad’s health. She said she lost about 20kg (44lb), her immune system weakened significantly, and doctors had to pause chemotherapy temporarily.

Al-Haj Ahmad is now receiving hormonal treatment while waiting to travel abroad for radiotherapy. Her referral for treatment abroad had been pending since September 2025.

Despite her own illness, she continues to examine women and refer suspected cases to the surgery department at Al-Aqsa Hospital. She also encourages women with a family history of breast cancer to be especially attentive to changes in their breasts.

“Early detection is especially important in Gaza because treatment options are so limited,” she said.

It has been a year since the “ceasefire” began in Gaza, although Israeli attacks continue, bringing the death toll from the war up to more than 74,400 Palestinians.

October is the global Breast Cancer Awareness Month – also known as Pink October. Health workers in Gaza are participating in the international initiative, with staff at Hekr al-Jameh Health Centre in Deir el-Balah trying to reach women through healthcare visits and targeted awareness sessions.

It’s part of a Pink October campaign they’ve called “pink blooms from among the rubble”, which teaches women about breast cancer, demonstrates breast self-examination, and offers psychological support to those affected by the disease.

Sabreen al-Buhaisi, who supervises Hekr al-Jameh’s primary healthcare services, said the centre had screened between 700 and 800 women during the campaign. Seven or eight cases were referred to hospital surgical departments for further assessment.

But identifying women who may have cancer is only the first step. Al-Buhaisi said free mammography was available at a limited number of hospitals, where women face long waits for appointments. Private screening is too expensive for many families.

“The financial cost is very high for women. Our people cannot afford these expenses,” she said.

Still, al-Buhaisi urged women to continue examining their breasts despite the difficult circumstances the vast majority live in.

“Even displacement and living in the camps should not stop you from examining yourself,” she said. “Take five minutes of your time. It can make a big difference in your treatment journey.”

Amid these hardships, Musbah continues her fight against time.

She says she has repeatedly followed up on the travel arrangements, but remains unable to leave, with no clear explanation for the delay.

The evacuation process is coordinated between the World Health Organization and Gaza’s Ministry of Health, but they have to then submit patients’ files to Israel for security screening and approval.

“I have been waiting for two years,” Musbah said. “And I still haven’t travelled.”

articles.title: Dementia risk may be linked to seemingly harmless daily habit, new research suggests
articles.summary: Even naps under 30 minutes raised dementia risk 40% in a Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health study of nearly 1,000 older adults.
articles.body: Frequent daytime napping among older adults has been linked to a higher risk of developing dementia, according to a study published in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences. Researchers from the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health tracked nearly 1,000 adults age 65 and older who showed no signs of memory or thinking problems when the study began in 2013. A decade later, the researchers found that daily rest habits — like how often people nap, how long they sleep and whether they fall asleep by accident — are linked to long-term brain health. ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES The study found that participants who napped frequently, defined as most days or every day, had a 48% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who rarely or never napped. Whether the naps were intentional also appeared to play a role. Seniors who fell asleep unintentionally had a 39% higher risk, while shorter naps were also linked to poorer outcomes. Napping for 30 minutes or less was linked to a 40% increased risk of dementia, even after researchers adjusted for other health factors. For naps longer than 30 minutes, the association was less pronounced after researchers accounted for nighttime sleep patterns. The research team stressed that looking at daytime napping habits gives a much clearer picture of overall health than looking at nighttime sleep alone. THIS ONE QUESTION MAY REVEAL WHETHER YOUR BODY IS GETTING THE REST IT NEEDS, STUDY FINDS "Our study highlights the importance of looking beyond just how long people nap and considering other napping characteristics, such as how frequently they nap and whether their naps are intentional," study authors Adam Spira, Ph.D., a professor at the Bloomberg School, and postdoctoral fellow Kening Jiang, Ph.D., told Fox News Digital. "This study provides important longitudinal evidence that frequent and unintentional daytime napping were associated with a higher risk of developing dementia among older adults." The findings held true even after accounting for nighttime sleep length, daytime drowsiness and indicators of sleep apnea. "Nighttime sleep and daytime napping are closely related," Spira and Jiang went on. "Daytime napping may compensate for poor nighttime sleep, but it may also reduce the drive to sleep at night, potentially contributing to nighttime sleep disturbances, another important potential risk factor for dementia." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Researchers pointed out that daytime resting does not necessarily cause brain changes. Rather, changing nap habits could be an early warning sign of underlying changes in the brain. Brain regions that help regulate wakefulness can start to break down in the early stages of dementia, leading to more frequent daytime fatigue, they noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES To double-check this, the team re-analyzed the data after removing anyone who developed dementia during the first five years. The link between frequent, accidental naps and dementia remained just as strong, suggesting that changes in napping habits can show up years before a formal diagnosis. The researchers emphasized that this was an observational study with limitations. "We did not directly intervene on participants’ napping behaviors to examine whether changing these behaviors would affect their dementia risk," Spira and Jiang told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Although we don’t know whether napping causes dementia, our study findings suggest that daytime napping patterns may be useful indicators of future dementia risk," they added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The findings suggest that daytime napping patterns in older adults may be worth monitoring, particularly when naps become frequent or happen unintentionally, according to the researchers.

articles.title: Top adviser to Kennedy resigns from Trump administration
articles.summary: Calley Means, a key adviser to health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and central advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, is leaving the Trump administration.
articles.body: Calley Means, a top adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and central advocate for the “Make America Healthy Again” movement, has resigned from the Trump administration. “I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and RFK — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Means said in a statement to NBC News. He posted a similar one on X. Means was an adviser on Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign and a key architect of his MAHA agenda. He joined the White House early last year as a special government employee. He transitioned to a full-time role as senior adviser to the Health and Human Services Department after divesting from his wellness company, Truemed. A person familiar with Means’ decision to resign said Means had been growing increasingly frustrated as he realized how little he could get done in Washington to advance his MAHA goals. The final straw, the source said, was the lack of progress on rolling out a federal definition of ultraprocessed foods — one of Means’ biggest priorities. The administration teased a definition in August but has yet to release it. The source also mentioned Trump’s executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S. (glyphosate is the key ingredient in Roundup), as well as some actions at the Environmental Protection Agency that have clashed with Kennedy’s agenda. Trump’s EPA has, for example, weakened mercury emissions standards and rolled back drinking water limits for certain PFAS chemicals — actions the MAHA movement has largely opposed. Frustrations over a lack of progress on MAHA goals have reverberated throughout the movement. Earlier this month, some supporters — including former members of Kennedy’s presidential campaign — accused the Trump administration of breaking nearly every promise made to them on food, agriculture and environmental health. With less than two weeks left until the midterm elections, some dissatisfied MAHA supporters have threatened to abstain from voting. Some Democrats are seeking to make inroads with the movement in the final days of campaigning. One of the MAHA movement’s central beliefs is that corporations hold too much influence over the food supply and healthcare system. Many of its supporters, including Means, had hoped to see a greater crackdown on pesticides and artificial dyes, as well as more significant changes to vaccine policy that emphasize what some describe as “medical freedom” over universal recommendations. On pesticides, a particular setback for the MAHA cause came in June, when the Supreme Court ruled that Bayer, the manufacturer of Roundup, didn’t need to warn consumers about a potential cancer risk associated with its product. The Trump administration had backed Bayer in the case. President Donald Trump last year nominated Means’ sister, Casey Means, for surgeon general, but she faced scrutiny at her confirmation hearing over her lack of an active medical license and past comments questioning the safety of vaccines and birth control. Trump chose a new nominee, Dr. Nicole Saphier, in April. Last month, at a talk Means gave at a MAHA summit in Washington, D.C., he said he was inspired by the way federal agencies had collaborated to advance the MAHA agenda, but he also acknowledged roadblocks. “D.C. is a tough place. It’s a toxic place, and there’s a lot of complaints you can make about D.C.,” Means said. “But I am more optimistic today than I’ve ever been about what I feel is my life’s work of evangelizing the chronic disease crisis and empowering Americans who want to be healthy to address the root cause of disease.” In his statement on Thursday, Means highlighted several policy wins for the MAHA movement during his tenure, including restricting soda purchases through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), fast-tracking research and review of psychedelics, urging food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and overhauling the federal dietary guidelines to recommend less ultraprocessed food and more protein. “More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history,” he wrote.

articles.title: France reports first human case of livestock virus Shamonda after patient dies
articles.summary: France reported the first human case of the Shamonda virus usually found in livestock on Thursday in a hospital patient who died, though authorities added there was no risk to the general population.
articles.body: France reported the first human case of the Shamonda virus usually found in livestock on Thursday in a hospital patient who died, though authorities added there was no risk to the general population. It is suspected that the victim was bitten by a midge carrying the virus in eastern France where it had circulated among animals this spring and summer, the government said in a statement. The man had been hospitalized in Lyon with an unrelated serious disease, a French health ministry official told reporters. The victim was in his 60s and lived in the Lyon area, local newspaper Le Progres reported. The UN’s World Health Organization said it was in contact with French authorities about the outbreak. “Based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this is an isolated human case and it is unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time,” said the Geneva-based WHO, which coordinates responses to international public health issues and emergencies. “We are clearly dealing with a case that is unprecedented from a scientific and virological point of view. It is linked to this man’s severely weakened immune system,” Gregory Emery, head of France’s health directorate, told reporters. “From a medical and public health point of view, there is no alert and no crisis,” he added. Shamonda is spreading in animals in Europe Shamonda is transmitted by biting midges and most commonly found in cattle, though it has also been found in horses, alpaca, sheep and goats, according to the World Organization for Animal Health. There has been no report of cattle-to-human or human-to-human transmission, Emery said. The virus is not classified as a disease under the EU Animal Health Law and not subject to official surveillance or control measures. Identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, Shamonda was first confirmed in Europe in late July after genomic tests on sick cattle in southern Germany, Switzerland and eastern France. France’s weekly animal health surveillance bulletin said it had also been detected in Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and Jersey. The virus has several effects on animals, with infected cattle showing diarrhea, weakness, loss of appetite and, less often, fever, French animal health authorities said. A study of nine French dairy farms found milk production fell by up to 75%.

articles.title: 9-year-old girl dies trying to save younger sister from drain in Khargone
articles.summary: 9-year-old Abha dies saving 4-year-old sister Kirti from drain in Khargone; villagers rescued Kirti, now stable. Police file unnatural death case.
articles.body: Khargone: A nine-year-old girl died while attempting to save her four-year-old younger sister after the two fell into a drain while playing near their home at Badgaon Ota in Kasrawad police station area of Khargone district on Thursday afternoon. The younger girl was rescued and admitted to hospital, where her condition was reported to be stable.According to Kasrawad police station in-charge Indresh Tripathi, the sisters were playing near their house when they went close to a nearby drain. Four-year-old Kirti fell into the muddy water, following which her elder sister, Abha, attempted to rescue her but got trapped in the mud.Villagers rushed to the spot and pulled both girls out. Abha had died by the time she was rescued, while Kirti was found in a serious condition and was rushed to govt hospital in Kasrawad.Dr Himanshi Patidar at the Kasrawad govt hospital said Abha was brought dead, while Kirti had water in her lungs. After receiving initial treatment, Kirti was referred to the district hospital for further care. Her condition was stable, the doctor said.Police reached the spot, conducted the inquest proceedings and registered a case of unnatural death (marg).
